newsitem.title: UK: Credit surge piles on pressure for UK rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Credit surge piles on pressure for UK rate hike.

text.p: Another surge in personal borrowing means the incoming Chancellor of the Exchequer after May 1 will have to raise British interest rates and probably by 50 rather than 25 basis points, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Consumer borrowing continues to grow at quite a healthy pace," said CIBC chief economist David Coleman.
"It keeps the pressure on whoever is the next Chancellor to raise rates just as the U.S. has done," he said.
Data published on Wednesday showed net consumer credit leapt by 1.22 billion pounds, the largest rise on record.
Analysts said the strong consumer credit was somewhat offset by the softer than expected growth in narrow money supply.
UK MO grew 6.4 percent in the year to March, less than the 6.5 percent forecast, despite a possible boost from the Easter weekend which fell seven days earlier than last year.
Morgan Grenfell analyst James Barty said more important was M4 growth, which was revised down to 11.2 percent from 11.3 for the year to February. This compared to 10.0 percent in January.
"The M4 number showed real money growth is now in excess of eight percent and that underlines why the economy is going to continue to strengthen over the rest of this year," said Barty.

Underlying inflation edged lower in February and is expected to fall further in the months ahead, but evidence of robust economic activity -- especially in the consumer sector -- is fuelling expectations a rate rise will have to come whichever way the May 1 election goes.
"There's no sign of inflation yet, but then there's no sign of inflation yet in the States and rates are going up there," said Coleman.

If opinion polls are right and the Conservative government is ousted by the Labour Party at the May 1 election, Britain's Chancellor Kenneth Clarke is likely to be replaced by Gordon Brown, the shadow finance minister.
Coleman said a new government could gain valuable credibility by raising rates by a half point.

"With a new government, there is an argument for a 50-point rise straight away -- getting the financial markets on your side with a tough policy and one that doesn't cost you anything in the first year of government."
